cim_eredeti: LangChain Tutorial: From Prompts to RAG and AI Agents
szoveg_eredeti:
LangChain is a framework for Python and JavaScript that lets you build applications powered by large language models (LLMs). Sending a single prompt to a model takes only a couple of lines of code. However, real apps also need reusable instructions, access to your own data, and a way for the model to call your Python code. In this tutorial, you’ll explore how LangChain’s Python library handles each of these.

Say a group of hospitals just handed you a spreadsheet full of patient reviews, together with a short request: Find out what patients are saying about us. You could read through every row yourself, but by the time you’re done, the next batch of reviews will probably have arrived. Instead, you’ll teach an LLM to do the reading for you.

Along the way, you’ll cover chat models, prompt templates, chains, retrieval, and agents. Step by step, you’ll build up to a RAG app that answers questions about what patients said and an agent that picks the right tool to look up exact facts.

To get the most out of this tutorial, you should be comfortable with Python functions, dictionaries, and comprehensions and have some familiarity with decorators and type hints. You don’t need any prior experience with LLMs, but a basic understanding of embeddings and vector databases will help in the RAG section. If you don’t have all of this background knowledge yet, that’s okay! You might learn more by going ahead and getting started.

Each section covers one feature. You’ll run most examples in the Python REPL and a few as scripts from the command line. You’ll start by preparing your environment and installing LangChain.

With this package, you can load environment variables from .env files into your Python environment. You’ll find this handy for keeping your API key out of your code.

You’ll use OpenAI’s models, so make sure you have an OpenAI account, a valid API key, and credits in your account. Running the examples in this tutorial might cost only a small amount, but every model and embedding call is billed.

Create a file called .env in your working directory and add your key to it:

Every script or REPL session in this tutorial calls dotenv.load_dotenv() to read the .env file and load your key into the environment before using any OpenAI model.

Note: Your .env file contains your API key in plain text. If your working directory is under version control, add .env to your .gitignore file so you don’t accidentally commit your key. If you commit your key and publish the repository, revoke the key and generate a new one.

You can run each section’s code on its own, but the concepts build on each other, so work through the sections in order if you’re new to LangChain. In the RAG and agent sections, you’ll create scripts and use reviews.csv from the tutorial’s materials.

You’re now ready to start exploring LangChain!

At the core of LangChain is the large language model (LLM) that powers its features. LangChain provides a modular interface for working with LLM providers, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Hugging Face, as well as local models. In most cases, all you need is an API key from the provider to start using the LLM with LangChain.

In LangChain, you talk to an LLM through a model object, such as ChatOpenAI or ChatAnthropic. Instead of sending raw text, you usually send the model a list of messages, which represent the input and output of models.

Every message object has .type and .content attributes. The .type attribute tells the LLM who is sending the message ("system", "human", or "ai"), and .content holds the message itself.

Note: In practice, you can refer to a SystemMessage as a system prompt and a HumanMessage as a user prompt. You can refer to an AIMessage as an AI response.

Under the hood, chat_model sends a request to OpenAI’s Responses API serving gpt-6-luna, and the response comes back as an AIMessage, as the call to type() confirms. You read the model’s reply from that message with its .text attribute.

As you can see, the chat model answers the question What is a normal resting heart rate? provided in the HumanMessage. You might be wondering what the chat model does with the SystemMessage in this context. Notice what happens when you ask the following question:

Your healthcare assistant stays in its lane! It won’t explain how to change a tire, but it still makes sure that you don’t get hurt while you wait for roadside assistance.

As described earlier, the SystemMessage tells the model how to behave. In this case, you tell the model to only answer healthcare-related questions, so it declines to walk you through the tire change. Using text instructions to control how an LLM interacts with the user is powerful and forms the foundation for creating customized chatbots through prompt engineering.
